The main challenge stems from the interaction between random regime shifts and portfolio non-negativity constraints, which typically causes the coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations to lose smoothness across different state regions. Additionally, directly imposing no-shorting constraints on randomized policies disrupts their analytically tractable Gaussian structure, complicating both exploratory modeling and reinforcement learning. To address these challenges, we propose an auxiliary exploratory approach that limits the policy to a Gaussian distribution and applies the no-shorting constraint solely to its mean. We explicitly characterize the optimal policy for this auxiliary problem and demonstrate that, by appropriately selecting the exploration variance, its optimal mean policy exactly matches the optimal policy of the original constrained mean-variance problem. Building upon this analytical framework, we develop a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the optimal portfolio policy directly from trajectory data. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and show that the proposed method can effectively recover the optimal no-shorting portfolio in a regime-switching market.
item.dc:creator: Minghui Zhang, Xun Li, Xin Zhang

item.title: BFGS can converge to non-Clarke-stationary points with positive probability
item.description: arXiv:2610.34087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct a coercive, locally Lipschitz, semialgebraic function on $\mathbb R^2$ for which BFGS with Armijo--Wolfe line search converges to a non-Clarke-stationary point from a nonempty open set of initial points and inverse-Hessian estimates. This disproves the almost-sure stationarity assertion in the 2013 challenge of Lewis and Overton. The construction and proof combine analytical arguments with computer-assisted verification of explicit inequalities.
item.dc:creator: Lexiao Lai

item.title: Split Cuts in Fixed Integer Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.02169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study how many split cuts are needed to reach the integer hull, and how large split closures can be. In every fixed dimension, a rational pure-integer polyhedron admits a polynomial-time constructible split proof of its integer hull with polynomial total encoding length; consequently, its full split rank is polynomial in the input length. This establishes the split-rank conjecture of Basu, Conforti, Di Summa, and Jiang for pure-integer polyhedra in fixed dimension. Central to our approach is a preservation result: in arbitrary pure-integer dimension, an inequality whose violating points map, under an affine map with integer coefficients, into the interior of a planar lattice-free polyhedron has a polynomial split proof retaining every point satisfying it. Whereas Chv\'atal--Gomory closures have polynomial-size inequality descriptions in fixed dimension, split closures need not: tetrahedra of input length $\Theta(\log N)$ can have split closures with at least $2N-1$ facets, yet extension complexity $\Theta(\log N)$. For the system $x=f+Rs$, $s\ge0$, $x\in\mathbb Z^2$ of input length $L$, the split closure has an exact extended formulation with $O(L)$ inequalities and auxiliary variables; this bound is tight. Separation over the split closure is polynomial-time in fixed total dimension. Finally, on mixed-integer feasible rational polytopes with fixed integer dimension $p$ and arbitrary continuous dimension, we optimize a primitive integral objective on the integer variables using $O_p(G+1)$ split cuts. Each cut removes a current optimal LP vertex, and the algorithm returns an optimal LP vertex that is mixed-integer feasible. $G$ is the integrality gap of the LP relaxation, rounded down.
item.dc:creator: Avinash Bhardwaj, Vishnu Narayanan

item.title: Unique continuation estimates for Baouendi--Grushin equations on cylinders
item.description: arXiv:2401.17782v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove time-pointwise quantitative unique continuation estimates for the evolution operators associated to (fractional powers of) the Baouendi--Grushin operators on the cylinder $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{T}^d$. Spectral inequalities are deduced, relating for functions from spectral subspaces associated to finite energy intervals their $L^2$-norm on the whole cylinder $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb T^d$ to the $L^2$-norm on so-called thick subsets of $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb T^d$. As a byproduct, we also obtain results on exact and approximate null-controllabilty for the corresponding evolution systems. This extends and complements results obtained recently by the authors and by Jaming and Wang.
item.dc:creator: Paul Alphonse, Albrecht Seelmann

item.title: The Spear and the Ring: Emergent Structures in Magnetic Colloidal Suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2504.02379v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study from a mathematical point of view the nanoparticle model of a magnetic colloid, presented by G. Klughertz. Our objective is to obtain properties of stable stationary structures that arise in the long-time limit for the magnetic nanoparticles dynamics following this model. In this article, we present a detailed study of two specific structures using techniques from the calculus of variations. The first, called the spear, consists of a chain of aligned particles interacting via a Lennard-Jones potential. We establish existence and uniqueness results, derive bounds on the distances between neighboring particles, and provide a sharp asymptotic description as the number of particles tends to infinity. The second structure, the ring, features particles uniformly distributed along a circle. We prove its existence and uniqueness and derive an explicit formula for its radius.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el C\^ote (IRMA, USIAS), Cl\'ementine Court\`es (IRMA, MACARON), Guillaume Ferriere (Paradyse), Ludovic Godard-Cadillac (UB, IMB, Bordeaux INP), Yannick Privat (IECL, SPHINX, IUF)

item.title: Observability estimates for the Schr\"odinger equation on the equilateral triangle
item.description: arXiv:2509.24642v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove observability estimates for the Schr\"odinger equation posed on the equilateral triangle in the plane, under both Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions. No geometric control condition is required on the rough localization functions that we consider. This is the first result of this kind on a non-toric domain in the compact setting. Our strategy is to exploit Pinsky's tiling argument to deduce this result from observability estimates on rational twisted tori. These are obtained via propagation of singularities, adapting arguments from Burq and Zworski. The later require Strichartz estimates on such twisted rational tori, that we derive from Zygmund inequalities in the same geometric setting, also providing the sharp constant. Strichartz estimates on the equilateral triangle are also derived from this analysis.
item.dc:creator: Paul Alphonse, David Lafontaine

item.title: Infinite-Time Mean Field FBSDEs and the Associated Elliptic Master Equations
item.description: arXiv:2510.03707v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study discounted infinite-time mean field forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) and the associated elliptic master equations, which were introduced in [20] as mathematical tools for solving discounted infinite-time mean field games. We first establish stability and flow properties, identify the backward decoupling field with the spatial derivative of the equilibrium value function, and prove that the value function is a viscosity solution of the master equation. Under additional smoothness and quantitative stability assumptions, we construct its Lions-derivative and the required higher-order derivatives using variational results from a companion paper [21]. These results show that the value function is a classical solution of the elliptic master equation. We also prove that the value function is the unique displacement-monotone regular solution.
item.dc:creator: Yongsheng Song, Zeyu Yang

item.title: Game-theoretic Regulated Decentralized Coordination for Airspace Sector Overload Mitigation
item.description: arXiv:2511.13770v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized air traffic management systems offer a scalable alternative to centralized control, but often assume high levels of cooperation. In practice, such assumptions frequently break down since agents, each representing an airspace sector, may operate independently and prioritize local objectives. We address the problem of sector overload in decentralized air traffic management by proposing a regulated decentralized protocol that models self-interested behaviors based on best response dynamics. Each agent adjusts the departure times of its assigned flights to reduce its own congestion, without requiring centralized joint optimization. A tunable cooperativeness factor models the degree to which each agent accounts for overload in other sectors, while a minimal admissibility rule prevents local updates from creating new overloads. We show that this regulatory restriction is sufficient to guarantee finite-time convergence of best response dynamics to a pure Nash equilibrium under partial cooperation. In addition, we identify a sufficient condition under which an overload-free solution corresponds to a global minimizer of the potential function. Numerical experiments using one month of European flight data demonstrate that the proposed algorithm substantially reduces overload even with only minimal cooperation, achieving performance close to a centralized global mixed-integer optimizer and exceeding a centralized first-come-first-served baseline while requiring substantially less computation than centralized optimization. We further evaluate departure delay and fairness to quantify the operational cost of overload mitigation.
item.dc:creator: Jaehan Im, Daniel Delahaye, David Fridovich-Keil, Ufuk Topcu

item.title: On-Line Policy Iteration with Trajectory-Driven Policy Generation
item.description: arXiv:2604.15004v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider deterministic finite-horizon optimal control problems with a fixed initial state. We introduce an on-line policy iteration method, which, starting from a given policy, however obtained, generates a sequence of cost-improving policies and corresponding trajectories. Each policy produces a trajectory, which is used in turn to generate data for training the next policy. The method is motivated by problems that are repeatedly solved starting from the same initial state, including discrete optimization and path planning for repetitive tasks. For such problems, the method is fast enough to be used on-line. Under a natural consistency condition, we show that the sequence of costs of the generated policies is monotonically improving for the given initial state (but not necessarily for other states). We illustrate our results with computational studies from combinatorial optimization and 3-dimensional path planning for drones and a robot arm in the presence of obstacles. We also discuss briefly a stochastic counterpart of our algorithm. Our proposed framework combines elements of rollout and policy iteration with flexible trajectory-based policy representations, and applies to problems involving a single as well as multiple decision makers. It also provides a principled way to train neural network-based policies using trajectory data, while preserving monotonic cost improvement.
item.dc:creator: Yuchao Li, Fei Chen, Yingke Li, Chuchu Fan, Dimitri Bertsekas

item.title: Welfarist Control Design - How to fulfill the societal mandate in multi-agent control?
item.description: arXiv:2606.23931v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: At the core of most socio-technical systems lies a scarce resource that is allocated among agents: highway lanes, public transit, road space, water rights, energy access, grid capacity, user attention, pollution rights, etc. With further automation of the underlying allocation processes, control engineers are increasingly tasked with making decisive assumptions regarding what society wants. In practice to date, design choices are largely driven by industry norms and conventions rather than a result of conscientiously responsible and ethical design. In this paper, we look at tools available to control engineers to design systems in a more principled manner in order to match the societal mandate. We consider three control design paradigms: online feedback optimization, control of Markov decision processes, and model predictive control. Beginning with aggregating individual agents' preferences into control design objectives, subsequently ensuring and certifying the fulfillment of those specifications, we argue that the feedback nature of control systems enables appropriate allocation of the shared resources in ways hitherto unparalleled.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Hall, Kai Zhang, Ilia Shilov, Heinrich H. Nax, Saverio Bolognani

item.title: Variable Bound Tightening for Nash Equilibrium Computation in Multiplayer Imperfect-Information Games
item.description: arXiv:2606.25997v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There has been significant recent progress in algorithms for approximation of Nash equilibrium in large two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games and exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer strategic-form games. While counterfactual regret minimization and fictitious play are scalable to large games and have convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games, they do not guarantee convergence to Nash equilibrium in multiplayer games. Recently, an approach has been presented for exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer imperfect-information games that solves a quadratically constrained program based on a nonlinear complementarity problem formulation derived from the sequence-form game representation. This formulation was solved using Gurobi's nonconvex quadratic solver, which employs spatial branch-and-bound to iteratively refine variable bounds by solving convex relaxations of bilinear terms. During presolve, Gurobi introduces auxiliary variables and, in some cases, binary variables, leading to an internal mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. This approach was demonstrated to outperform prior algorithms from the Gambit software suite and quickly solve three-player Kuhn poker after removal of dominated actions; however, the algorithm was not able to solve the full version of the game within 24 hours. In this paper, we derive finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables in the nonlinear complementarity formulation. These bounds can strengthen the convex relaxations used within spatial branch-and-bound. We compare uniform corollary bounds with finer proposition-based bounds on full three-player Kuhn poker. All eight bounded configurations return numerically verified equilibria in under 17 seconds, while the unbounded formulation finds no feasible solution within 300 seconds. The finest bounds do not consistently yield the fastest computation.
item.dc:creator: Sam Ganzfried

item.title: Recovery Theory for Projected Power Iterations in Permutation Synchronization
item.description: arXiv:2609.09502v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the projected power method for permutation synchronization: recovering $n$ unknown permutations of $m$ objects from pairwise relative permutations, observed independently with probability $p$ and independently corrupted by uniform permutations with probability $1-\pi_0$. Our main theorem establishes uniform one-step contraction for all estimates with optimally aligned block-error fraction at most $1/2-\epsilon$, for fixed $\epsilon>0$, including measurement-dependent estimates. When $np\ge C_0\log(n)$ and $m=o(np\pi_0^2)$, one update contracts the error by a factor $O(m/(np\pi_0^2))$, up to a floor of $O(e^{-c\min\{m\,np\pi_0^2,\,np\pi_0\}} + \log(n) / n)$. Thus, every initialization in this majority basin achieves $o(1)$ error after one update and maintains it uniformly over subsequent iterations. A reference-block spectral initializer enters the basin with probability $1-o(1)$, yielding end-to-end almost-exact recovery. If additionally $\min\{m\,np\pi_0^2,\,np\pi_0\} \ge C\log(n)$ for sufficiently large $C$, the method achieves exact recovery in finitely many iterations. We also establish prescribed-block recovery under weaker conditions for measurement-independent estimates and extend the guarantees to independent permutation-valued corruptions with uniform mean and to partial permutations with common visible support.
item.dc:creator: Vahan Huroyan, Gilad Lerman

item.title: Optimal defective chromatic separation for clique blowups
item.description: arXiv:2609.17557v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld conjectured that colouring the \((d+1)\)-clique blowup of a graph with defect \(d\) requires as many colours as colouring the graph properly. Norin and Steiner refuted this, proved that the two chromatic numbers differ by at most a factor of two, and asked for the exact constant; the best separation known was \(11/10\). We prove that the constant is exactly two for every fixed defect \(d\ge 2\). Every rational ratio in \([1,2)\) is attained, by graphs whose clique number and fractional chromatic number equal the defective parameter: the separation is invisible to the standard lower bounds. The engine is an exact transfer theorem: a weighted list-colouring obstruction spread over an arbitrary auxiliary graph yields prescribed defective and ordinary chromatic numbers; Kneser graphs then give sharpness. A 29-vertex graph with defective parameter four and chromatic number five answers Norin's Barbados question at the smallest possible defect and palette.
item.dc:creator: Guillaume Lecomte

item.title: Interpretable Cutting Plane Selection for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Using Genetic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2610.29311v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cutting planes (cuts) remove fractional solutions from mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) without excluding any feasible integer solutions, making them a key ingredient in modern MILP solvers. Current state-of-the-art solvers rely on fine-tuned handcrafted cut strategies, which, despite their effectiveness, remain inherently static and can be suboptimal. More recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to design adaptive cut strategies; however, most of these methods are based on neural networks, offering limited interpretability and providing no guarantees of convergence. In this paper, we propose \emph{Genetic Programming and Statistics-based Cut Selection} (GPSCS), the first learning-based framework that explicitly generalizes handcrafted cut selection heuristics into a fully interpretable policy. First, a genetic programming model evolves a symbolic scoring function that ranks candidate cuts using features derived from the cuts and the solving context. Second, a lightweight statistics-based mechanism adaptively determines the number of top-ranked cuts to add at each separation round by detecting significant score dropouts. We evaluate GPSCS within the SCIP solver on seven classes of synthetic and real-world benchmark instances, with a strong emphasis on generalization: evaluation instances are on average 41 times harder than those used for training. Experimental results show that GPSCS improves average solving time by $6\%$ compared to SCIP's default cut selection strategy and achieves a two-fold speedup over both a recent neural-network-based approach and a no-cut baseline, demonstrating strong robustness and generalization across heterogeneous MILP families.
item.dc:creator: Gwen maudet, Mathis Da Cunha, Gr\'egoire Danoy

item.title: First- and second-order constrained optimisation for inverse homogenisation of unidirectionally varying microstructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.03372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper is concerned with inverse homogenisation problems that aim to identify microstructure features of a body from macroscopic measurements. The unknown microstructure is assumed to vary macroscopically in one spatial direction and affects the effective tensor in an elliptic partial differential equation that governs the behaviour of the body on the macroscale. We establish the well-posedness of the PDE-constrained minimisation problems that model the task of identifying the microstructure, derive first-order necessary optimality conditions, and prove the convergence of a gradient-projection algorithm for the studied problem class in an infinite-dimensional setting. We moreover demonstrate that recently obtained results on generalised differentiability properties of solution maps of bilateral obstacle problems make it possible to set up and analyse a novel semismooth Newton method in the considered situation. The functional analytic setting that we use for our investigation is chosen such that it covers various elliptic PDEs simultaneously (classical second-order equations, bi-Laplace problems, linear elasticity, etc.) and explicitly exploits the problem structure to obtain global convergence guarantees for the studied solution algorithms in terms of the Lipschitz constants of the involved operators. Our analysis is accompanied by numerical experiments which show that the new semismooth Newton approach requires far less expensive projection evaluations than the gradient-descent method and, thus, offers a significant speedup.
item.dc:creator: Constantin Christof, Malte A. Peter, Michael Ulbrich
